As someone who has helped to secure critical national infrastructure several years ago, I can say that it was a mess to disclose the vulnerabilities I identified, and in some cases it took years to patch them. Some of these vulnerabilities were RCEs and mass PII leaks. It's simply not worth the risk for most people - who aren't in the USA - to bother doing this sort of security research. However, if you are in the USA, there are provisions in the CFAA that enable good-faith security research to take place (https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/department-justice-a...), so to the best of my understanding, you're able to do good-faith research without being charged or prosecuted, and you should take advantage of this if you have the skills or models to do so. I am not based in the USA, and there are no laws in my country that guarantee me zero jail time for simply trying to do the right thing, so I am not incentivized to continue finding vulnerabilities in my country's infrastructure.

Edit: If other countries don't catch up and include similar provisions in their laws, they'll simply fall behind and put their citizens at risk. I'm sure every country has individuals willing to help that currently feel unsafe - look at the large amount of bug bounty hunters worldwide who, I'm sure, wouldn't mind practicing their skills by securing their country's infrastructure.

> ...is there a future where we end up with a version of the open web where everything isn’t paywalled or ID gated?

Absolutely! When OpenAI and Anthropic fail to secure enough funding to keep operating, the VCs backing the customers from which most of their money comes from will turn off the money faucets. This will dramatically reduce the amount of money being spent on the attack^Wover-exuberant scraper bots, which will drop that noise down dramatically.

Once folks aren't paying out the ass to serve up data for bots that really never use it, then a lot of the folks who have built or are building walls now will be able to tear them down.

Also, a great alternative to providing a government-issued photo ID and/or live biometrics is for Web Services to be obligated to use a government-provided categorizing scheme to categorize the things that their service provides and does, for major OS providers to be obligated to allow a local system administrator to set categories of things that certain accounts on that system cannot see or do, and then for the major web browser producers, people-who-publish-in-"app stores", and Web Service providers to be obligated to honor those sysadmin-configured restrictions.

This is really good because not only does it not require anyone to provide an ID and/or biometrics to some cut-rate third-party vendor, [0] but it allows -for example- both typical twelve-year-olds as well as dementia-damaged adults to be protected. The current systems pretend that every XXX-year-old is pretty much identical, and that zero people over the age of seventeen will ever need to be protected, which are obviously untrue things.

[0] ...who is 100% going to inevitably lose control of a large fraction of that data...

comment_text.value:
> User agent strings are a sad consequence of websites incorrectly parsing them to enable functionality, resulting in a "every bug becomes a contract" type of situation.

Which is precisely why trying to legislate them is folly. Obviously the reason Android calls itself "Mobile Safari" is so that servers send it the mobile version of the site instead of the desktop one etc.

Which makes "accurate" an unreasonable requirement, since there is already a preexisting non-waivable requirement for inaccurate. When someone is making their "turn a web page into a PDF so you can view it later on the plane" software or whatever, it has to use a user agent string that will cause the site to send the version you need turned into the PDF.

> That being said, if you include GOOGLEBOT in your 1k long query string, alongside a very long page describing your crawlers, how to identify them, how to block them and how to set limits, no judge will find you guilty of concealing your purpose.

First, you're assuming that the person being prosecuted is the entities who are the nominal targets of the bill, when the real problem is when they're not. Because you're proposing a law that says anybody with an inaccurate user agent string is in violation, meanwhile everybody has an inaccurate user agent string.

Moreover, consider what you expect the outcome of legislating something like this is going to be. Sites could then try to either blacklist or whitelist user agents.

If they do the first one, that doesn't work, because the scraping service can change it whenever they want.

If they do the second one, that doesn't work, because now every third party has to start pretending to be a common browser even when they're doing something totally innocent or they get blocked by default for being something else. Which makes the user agent string even less useful than it is now, and subjects innocent parties to arbitrary liability for doing something they have to do or their client is broken.

> As for why the law is written as is instead of banning more specific functionality, it's so assholes don't get any ideas on how to bypass it.

You're describing autocracy. The way you make it so that you always prosecute someone is to make it so that you can always prosecute anyone, which is very bad.

>I don't quite get the difference, patients pay a fixed amount for insurance, hospitals charge "fee for service" to the insurance. Both systems coexist, it's not one or the other.

I think their reference to "per capita" here is referring to a capitated payment structure where a provider organization is given a fixed amount per patient up front instead of billing for every service they provide. The software analog would be something like a flat subscription fee vs usage-based billing. While it's not the default in the US, it theoretically encourages providers to provide cost-effective care rather than just racking up bills on unhealthy patients.

The mechanism here is who bears the financial risk. The model you're familiar with is one where the payer (commercial insurance or medicare/medicaid) is the risk-bearing entity. They want more cost-effective care so they can protect their margins while the provider is incentivized to push a high volume of expensive care so they can boost their margins. Don't have it handy but the data on this shows providers are winning this battle with healthier, growing margins vs insurance companies whose margins generally aren't great.

comment_text.value:
TFA also offers no support for the assertion she's a "spy" vs just a source. When most people hear "spy" they think of a "Non-Official Cover" agent (aka NOC in the biz) with training, a false identity and a directed mission. But those are actually extremely rare. The vast majority of 'spying' is not done by 'spies' in that sense. It's basic information gathering from normal people who are already in a job which puts them in casual contact with a person, company or agency of interest.

There are literally thousands of these 'sources' for every NOC on a targeted mission. Many of these sources aren't even paid, they're just predisposed to be friendly to the nation who wants the info and willing to pass along things they see or hear in exchange for a favor or access. Most of what they pass along is irrelevant and useless impressions or chatter but it's all captured and cross-referenced by analysts.

When Jensen makes a two day visit to some Asian country like Singapore, he probably has over a dozen meetings including various local employees, distributors, vendors, govt agencies or media contacts. Nvidia's posture and distribution plans in Asia are of great interest to China, since they're trying to divert a good chunk of those GPUs to China. I have no doubt the Chinese (and other intel agencies) got reports from over half a dozen different sources regarding what happened during Jensen's visit.

Jensen is very smart and has a lot of experience. He knows he's a high-value target and everyone is info gathering on him. Hypothetically, even if he was banging the hot, young distributor rep when visiting Singapore (and I doubt he is), she wouldn't get any actionable intel. Not because she might send an email report to Chinese intelligence but because she'll certainly give a detailed report to her bosses at the distributor. All of NVidia's distributors are trying to glean any competitive insight or favor from NVidia they can.

> But aren't there additional systems that can detect that a block is obstructed (e.g. also by left behind carriages that got disconnected) like the electrical track circuit (Gleisstromkreis)?

That's not an additional system, that is the PZB (or here ASFA).

> Or wouldn't that have helped because we're back again to the issue that with the downgrade from LZB to PZB we lost the virtual blocks, and both trains are now occupying the same, longer, non-virtual block?

Yes.

> But they have no indication that there is a second train (Iryo) in front, occupying the same block.

We don't know what they missed, and speculating on that is quite pointless, if we want to have that discussion, we need to wait for the post mortem, this is what such a report exists for. We only know THAT they missed something. That they missed that the first train was in that block too, is one option. It could also be, that it was not clear which signals are virtual or that there was a communication mismatch between different dispatchers or that there was a bug in the automatic train identification system or that an automatic system did call for that procedure. All of these already do occur in railway accidents, they are not really speculative. The last one is what happened in 2002 in the exact same situation: the computer automatically ordered the second to full speed and the first to stop. There could also be some other issue, that I can't think of right now. Most likely it's more than one error, because people still do pay attention.

> Hence, I assume, the protocol to resume operations with drive by sight after a LZB failure (which seems to have been ignored in this case)

I don't actually know what the protocol in Spain is. In Germany it is like that now, but only due to the 2002 near-accident. Before that it was ambiguous. If you are a dispatcher you don't only get taught a bunch of rules. You get taught the primary constraints and then you are able to construct the rules from first principles. However under pressure it's likely to forget something vital, so there are still rules that you are supposed to follow. But no ruleset will be ever complete, that's why you don't only follow rules.

> But why not also have the protocol demand that operations are resumed front-to-back in that situation?

That wouldn't solve anything. Drive by sight is safe in that situation, driving faster is not. If you start front-to-back you can still have collisions, but you just waste time. There is also not necessarily no physical block between trains, so it could be safer to start a later train. Also are you sure you are able to correctly assess the positions and order of the train? You are supposed to, but I mean that obviously failed here. Just drive by sight.

I can't speak to the GUI, just the TUI compared to tmux.

herdr is very flexible, but it shines when you are working with multiple projects, with multiple worktrees, and multiple agents within those projects.

1. herdr uses workspaces to help organize tabs. Conceptually, a workspace probably maps to a project, but it doesn't have to.

2. herdr has native worktree support, and can create a nested workspace per worktree with a keyboard or CLI command. It can check out worktrees for you

3. herdr identifies agents across tabs and workspaces and pulls them out into an extra navigational pane. It shows the status of those agents (e.g. idle, working, waiting, done), and can play a sound when they change state. This helps you track multiple agents across multiple projects and quickly switch to them when they need help without needing to remember "claude is running in space 2, tab 3"

4. herdr integrates with your agents, which can control herdr's UI and rename tabs based on their status.

5. All this is scriptable via the herdr CLI, and agents are very good at it. But it also has full mouse support, if you're new to multiplexers its very easy to start interacting with it.

comment_text.value:
I also never understood this desire to build an agent org chart with persistent identities, often giving them names. Paperclip seems to advertise that model. I think it's much simpler and more flexible to simply spawn an agent for each task.

One argument for the persistent identity model is that you can give them special skills and context. I don't believe that's a good argument. In my experience, you can just give each agent access to the full set of tools (including RAG search) in the form of documentation and skills, and they'll use that efficiently. Skills have a tiny front matter and hardly bloat the context, and the documentation just needs to be tree-structured with cross-links for progressive disclosure. LLMs navigate that efficiently, so the cost of having all context accessible is low, while the risk of cutting the context boundaries for the persistent identities non-optimal for a given task is rather high IMO.

comment_text.value:
I'll take a crack at this one. I've been using matrix and element for over a decade as my main messenger, and it's great, but it also does suck. I even use it for my business chat. It's pretty much the most popular federated encrypted client right now, and it seems to have taken over XMPP's lead. So here's a nice list/rant about why matrix/element sucks.

1. I spent 15 minutes last month helping my business partner sign onto ElementX on his second phone. He's signed on his PC and his primary phone, but the second phone was very difficult. Basically type username and password, but now you have to verify with emoji. How do you do that? Well, sometimes it pops up on your other clients that a new client needs verification. Sometimes the popup never shows, and there's no way to find it. But we found it eventually. Verify via emoji. Great! Let's do it. Oops, it timed out before he could finish. Apparently it has a super short timer that even I struggle with it. Eventually we gave up and used the recovery key, which worked, but you know many people are going to lose that key since it's not a password they can just memorize. Most other messengers, it's just username, password, and then click the email confirmation link. Boom, easy.

2. Audio/Video calling/conferencing. There are apparently 3(?) different technologies in Element alone, depending on which version of Element (desktop, web, mobile). The "old" one is jitsi. The new p2p one appears to be only available to clients that aren't Element? Or you can only create conference rooms in those other clients (commet?), but you can join them from any client. But then those new rooms are sometimes not join-able from Element clients. They just don't appear in the room list at all. Even clicking a link to the room says it's the wrong "room version", but it's a freshly-created room. So I delete the room and make another new one. But now it's a Jitsi room and it doesn't work in this other Element client (all first-party actual Element clients, and all broken in slightly different ways!). So... it's working now, but only after lots of trial and error and lots of cussing from my business partner. And I have to somehow justify that this is better than using Slack/Discord/whatever corporate thing.

3. The official client is fragmented. On mobile, there is Element (classic) and ElementX. You're _supposed_ to use ElementX, since it's the new one, but ElementX does not have all the features of Element (classic), so you might need the Element (classic) client for those things. But Element (classic) is not getting updated, so you're left in the cold as far as updates and the new features (meaning you might not even be able to cross-verify your clients, or join video calls, spaces, etc.)

4. The official matrix server (synapse) is pretty slow. I hosted a couple small communities (~100 people or so?), and synapse somehow kept getting overloaded and crashing. Maybe it needed more than 4GiB, but that seems kind of silly. There are decent 3rd-party clients (continuwuity is my current favorite), but there's no migration path from one server to another without wiping your entire database and starting fresh. So.... my main homeserver is kind of stuck on synapse.

5. Bridges. Yes, you can bridge anything to anything, but have you actually tried it? Interface is super clunky. You have to run a separate bridge service, make sure it swaps keys with the matrix server via a yaml configuration dance, then talk to the bridge's bot in a dedicated matrix channel with special commands that may or may not get your bridge working. I've used signal, discord, telegram, and irc bridges, and they're all a mess in one way or another. My most recent attempt was with the signal bridge. I made the mistake of enabling end-to-end encryption. One day, the bridge server restarted and lost all its encryption keys. Cool, now all the bridged rooms are dead. So naturally, I delete the bridge service and re-configure it from scratch. Now it doesn't work because its bridge bot username was already taken by the previous instance with the lost encryption keys. And I can't just delete that bridge bot user because _matrix does not allow deleting users ever!_. So now I have broken signal bridge rooms and broken signal bot users that I can't ever delete, even with the admin panel. So naturally I open up a postgresql client and delete them manually. Oops, now my matrix database is broken in ways I cannot even begin to comprehend. Because deleting users is not allowed. So now I just can't have a signal bridge. _maybe_ there's a way to make it work, but I've been programming and sys-admin'ing for over 20 years, and it's just beyond me. I'm going to have to (again!) wipe out my homeserver and start over, losing all my messages and contacts (again!). XMPP had very nice transport services, and Psi+ had a very nice UI for configuring and organizing them.

6. Multi-identity support is lacking in all the official and most community clients. If I have a work account and a personal account, I need to start two separate Element clients. Each one is a hefty electron app, and they all have the same systray icon, so I need to trial+error every time to open the right one to message someone. So far, there's only one client I tried that had proper multi-account, and I think it was commet. It was ok, but I hated that it was a flutter desktop app where every click felt super unresponsive. So I went back to Element. Most XMPP clients have multi-identity built-in. I'm not going to use my work identity for personal chat, just like I'm not going to use my hackernews account to message co-workers.

7. No message auto-deletion. Many people like to claim that Element is more secure than Signal. It is not. If you live in an oppressive country where things you say can easily result in prison or torture, you need more than E2E encryption. You need messages to be gone. You can't trust that your device or your friend's device won't get confiscated and forced to reveal your password. Even the United States has forced device unlocking at the borders. Signal (and Confide, and even Telegram) have automatically deleting messages, so even with the keys, there's nothing to see. Matrix stores messages forever. Aside from some complicated server-side setting, there's no way to automatically delete them. You have to right-click and manually delete EVERY message if you want future privacy. Nobody's going to do that. And I tried enabling the synapse settings for auto-deleting messages, but they didn't work. It seems that feature isn't really tested, or it's documented poorly.

8. The spam/CSAM problem when running a public community. The admin tools are a bit lacking, so without some considerable expertise, it's often not worth even having a community matrix server. So folks just make a discord instead, which has actual moderation tools builtin. Yes, I know there are external moderation tools you can install, but why should that be required?

9. The protocol is too complex to make full-featured 3rd-party clients. This isn't IRC where you can make a basic client in 3 lines of perl. You'll notice that the 3rd-party clients are all lacking in some features of Element, the official client. Even the official ElementX client lacks features of Element Classic. Most folks are stuck on the official electron-based Element client, which has a fairly clunky UX (try explaining to your grandma how to cross-verify clients).

This list is just off the top of my head. I could probably write a whole book on the problems with the matrix ecosystem. But again, matrix is the best we have. IRCv3 hasn't really caught on, and the need for an IRC bouncer to receive offline messages isn't commonly excepted in 2026. XMPP was/is ok, but it hasn't been commonly used since Google Hangouts pulled the bait+switch on us 10+. I keep thinking I should really just go back to XMPP, or start using delta.chat since "everyone" has an email address.

I often can't even get fairly technical folks (who write code by hand, etc) to use Element, even if I do all the server setup and just hand them the keys. It's too hard for most folk. It's too hard for me, and I've been maintaining my own matrix servers for 7+ years. I maintain 3 matrix servers right now. One synapse, and two continuwuity. NixOS makes it pretty easy to maintain servers, actually, as long as they're not open to the public.

And if anyone asks me "what should we use instead?", I'd probably say XMPP or IRC. And we know neither of those is perfect, either, and nothing open source and federated is as easy to onboard like Discord, Signal, or Slack.

But even though Element/Matrix sucks, it still works well enough for me to use it as my main communication. At least until I finish my own multi-protocol messenger. Which I started about 6 years ago and haven't had time to work on.

Disclosure: I wrote some of the code on Confide's backend back in 2021. I do not currently work at that company and am not promoting or un-promoting the app in any way.

I read a lot of old material from 1-1900AD where I can pick upon the author's 'voice'. There are subtle clues, like if they had a regional accent, where they use a specific word or type of cadence.

AI does the same with responses where the cadence is some type of formula that becomes identifiable.

Each of the big models has their own but an example of the cadence is

A) Agreement or Acknowledgement with the User

B) Specific detail gets a paragraph of detail related to the previous response

C) Overview of the conversation's current state

D) Prompting or Direction for this conversation to go

E) Landing on a beat. Wrap up the vibe. Recap with a zinger.

I cannot unsee it and a few of the models are annoying. I have attempted to build out the Agents and context to avoid the 'last beat one liner' without success because after 2-3 more turns, I get "That challenge was accepted and you stepped up. You're the winner this round".

Firstly, take everything that I say with a grain of salt. I can only reply on to the things that you've told here and give advice from it but I don't know the full situation. Read the advice and apply it as you wish.

> I have been staying up late, sleeping in, skipping chores, neglecting my relationships, eating too much food, neglecting hygiene, and generally just being a bum.

Happens with me. Something which helps me is figuring out why I sleep late. For me, it was a constant cycle of trying to do something today's night to cope up with waking up late or not doing something today.

Realize that productivity = hours put in * focus. I found myself constantly procastinating (hours go down) and when doing tasks (with less focus)

And if you continue this cycle, then the cycle continues. Over a long term, it is better for you to sleep today no matter how the day went early and then wake up early. It has been scientifically shown to improve your mental health and even from the logical standpoint of productivity, it will be better to sleep early today than not.

Your time is constant, when you sleep late you are borrowing time from tomorrow's productivity and this borrowing cycle will continue and you will feel as if you are short on time but you have ample amount of time provided you break the cycle.

Don't Neglect your relationships: Here's a comment[0] that I recently wrote about it. TLDR: try to appreciate them back and don't take them for granted. Appreciate them a lot.

There is some logic that I have found in that struggle is finite and constant and you can either take it in small doses today rather than an instant hit later. This also applies to doing chores

Regarding cleanliness: My room is a mess but the logic which can help is that I have found myself losing so so many time because I lost my keys or just lost something and then it has an insane amount of stress/time loss and struggle. I had forgotten (twice) that I had already taken my clothes back from laundry because of how messy my room is and I had to manually count all clothes I have (twice).

The amount of struggle in keeping your room clean is better than keeping it not clean.

Also, even speaking out of logical arguments, right now if I understand you, you want to be the guy who does keep his room clean, who does sleep early and who does appreciate relationships. You don't want the immediate benefits of it as much as you want it to help be part of your identity and boost its self-confidence. You want to be the guy as you want to do something, anything.

> My main reason has been that I am afraid of interviewing and that my skills are not up to par.

Happens with me as well but again the struggle is constant if not larger. You can either do interviews right now and fail them (which is okay, literally everyone fails) and failure teaches more than success. You learn from it, you improve and your fear can be taken less. Fear is because of the fact that you aren't approaching it, not that you aren't approaching it because of fear. In some sense, its a chicken and egg problem and the only way to break out of it is to not give the fear enough importance to make you change decisions but rather act on it and pass through its struggle and win through it. Worst case: you don't get the job, best case: you do.

comment_text.value:
I like where you're trying to go, but I'm afraid that you might have a chicken/egg problem on your hands. You need an oracle for the soulbound identities, which requires a widely supported coalition, but to get such a coalition despite incumbents who would divide it, you need the tool to already work.

I figure the tools of the successful revolutionary become the tools of the new government, so whatever it is it's gotta be useful for a small minority that wants to coordinate in the face of a sophisticated adversary, and then once it grows up it's gotta be useful for carrying out the bureaucratic business of a government. Unless it survives that transition with its trustworthiness intact, it won't be seen by the masses as trustworthy enough for the job. People just aren't that keen on trusting computers on the say-so of nerds like us, they need to see it succeed under stress.

So for starters I imagine an ocean of Sybil identities controlled by an enemy. Some of these will be trying to get info about your intentions so they can interfere (polling of one kind). Also you'll need to coordinate with comrades without making your entire trust graph known to all parties (polling of the other kind).

It'll never get to the point where coalitions are large if it doesn't function well when they're small, and at that phase you gotta be choosy about who you share info with because you're not yet a government but rather a threat to the existing one.

But OIDC was pretty explicitly designed for this (at least the later versions) - The whole point is that you can configure an identity provider, and then outsource identity verification to that provider.

So sure - it wasn't designed with agents directly in mind, but it's supported workload identity federation for a while (and is used in this manner for lots of big players - github, GCP, AWS, Azure, etc...)

What you're saying here is different than what you implied in the first comment.

There is a real and meaningful difference between

1. A user can blame a rogue agent for actions they [the user] performed

2. An agent itself went rogue

So sure - #2 is still a risk, and one they'd have to mitigate with the security controls they talked about (minimal access, temporary grants, HITL, etc). Frankly - #2 is always a risk. That's what "agents" are (both the bot and the fleshy kind). It's also why we have logging and visibility tools that should be recording what was done, by whom, and for what reason, along with robust backups. You can't really close this hole, you accept it, monitor it, and hold the agent to account (and again - I'm with you on discussing culpability for bots and what that means in the legal sense. Ex - do we charge the person who introduced the bot, the company running it, the party that injected bad context, etc...?)

But #1 is not a thing a person can do - they can't take malicious actions and then blame a rogue agent.

Hi HN, I'm Graeme. popkern is a free, open-source parametric BRep CAD kernel in Rust. You can try it in your browser here, no install: https://popkern.dev/live/ (I recommend checking out the six-axis robot arm example near the end of the examples list, it's 57 parts and ~1,200 features, all built from script). popkern is currently released under AGPL-3.0, with an exception so your scripts, models, and STEP files remain entirely yours.

The thing I'm proudest of: where several fillets of different radii meet at a corner, most kernels leave a curvature break you can see in reflections. popkern fills those corners with a certified G2 (curvature-continuous) patch, so zebra stripes flow through unbroken: https://popkern.dev/assets/img/zebra-corner.png

Other bits that might be interesting:

- Parts are short Rhai scripts. Bigger parts are folders of numbered "migration" scripts, like database migrations, so models are git-friendly and you can scrub through their history. A later step can reach back and modify an earlier feature.

- The model viewer in popkern live allows you to see into the model via a section view.

- All supported: booleans, fillets/chamfers, sweeps, revolves, lofts, shelling, constrained sketches, STEP in/out, and MCP for direct agent usage.

- When an operation can't produce a valid solid, it refuses and tells you why instead of returning something broken.

How it's built: the code is written by AI agents working from published CAGD research, under my direction. I spend a lot of my time reviewing research to identify solutions that close gaps. Every change must pass thousands of tests plus the kernel's own validity checks, and results are cross-checked against OpenCASCADE wherever the two are comparable. Happy to go deep on how that works.

What's missing: a lot, it's early. Booleans fail many tricky cases, and non-manifold topology is being built out right now. Similarly, the breadth of fillet support will grow over time, and there is much to improve with regards to surface healing. Fuzz testing for all three of these areas will be tackled soon and help harden popkern a great deal.

I hope people find it useful even this early, and I’d love to hear what breaks. Happy to answer questions.

The shared-API-key failure mode here is classic: once the agent “acts as” the same credential, authorization becomes binary (“does the key work?”) instead of contextual (“is this user allowed to do this action?”). The hard parts aren’t authentication—they’re policy enforcement and provenance.

A few things to sanity-check / ask about in any solution:

1. *Where is authorization enforced?* If the CRM/billing side only sees one API key identity, then the enforcement has to happen before requests leave your system (an authorization gateway), not “inside the agent” at best-effort level.

2. *Do you achieve least privilege per user?* Ideally: user-specific tokens (scoped OAuth, per-user API tokens, or a token exchange that mints short-lived credentials with constrained scopes). If not possible, you need an explicit mapping of user → allowed operations → resource set and block everything else.

3. *Strong auditability / attribution (“who did what?”).* You want logs that can answer, after the fact: user X initiated action Y on resource Z at time T, and which policy decision produced it. If all you record is “the shared credential called endpoint /charges”, you’ll struggle when banks/investors/auditors ask for evidence.

4. *Confused-deputy and prompt-injection controls.* Multi-user agents are basically “capability routers” for untrusted inputs. You need to treat the agent as potentially tricked and ensure policy checks are independent of the model’s output. Practical controls: structured tool calls, server-side validation of parameters against policy, and disallowing free-form “apply changes” operations.

5. *Resource-level authorization, not just action-level.* “User can update invoices” isn’t enough—you usually need “user can update their invoices/customers.” That implies resource ownership/tenant mapping and consistent ID normalization.

6. *Approvals and reconciliation for high-risk actions.* For destructive or money-moving operations, require an approval step and keep a reversible trail (request → approval → execution → final receipt).

If you’re replying to the “shared key” scenario, I’d be curious how you handle: - user-to-resource mapping (tenant/customer ownership), and - whether every outbound request is intercepted for policy checks with deterministic logs, rather than relying on the agent’s behavior.

Most “access control for agents” demos skip one of those, and that’s where incidents come from.

If you leave the door to your house unlocked, am I welcome to come in, pop on into your utility closet, plug into a switch port and take everything your machines allow me to fetch?

I don't disagree with what he was doing from a moral standpoint or a hacker standpoint, but it's very easy to convict him.

This discussion typically devolves into an argument about what is "publicly accessible." No reasonable person (i.e. those who serve on juries - not autistic software engineers) would agree that someone who isn't even a student at a school is legally entitled to enter a building (unlocked or not), venture into their utility room and access protected computer resources.

Everyone loves to make this about JSTOR: they weren't the only victim. MIT was far more aggrieved; JSTOR blocking his Harvard account access and him proceeding to breach their TOS ("clickwrap agreements aren't law!!!") and circumvent their defenses isn't required to convict him of CFAA violations.

Why can't I go into a bank, sit down at a personal banker's desk who is away on vacation, plug into a switch port and do whatever I want? There's no lock on his cubicle, the door was open! This is the legal equivalent of "neener neener, I'm not touching you."

Mens rea is an important thing people love to sweep under the rug with this case:

• First and foremost: Why did he have to go to into a closet at MIT to fetch documents? Why not do it at home or a public library?

  • Because of rate limits and/or authentication requirements. He *knew* he could not obtain the access he needed through other means, so he had to trespass to do it.
• Why did he cover his face with his bicycle helmet... just when passing by cameras?

  • He wasn't some weirdo who liked to wear his helmet that way: he stopped immediately when he believed he didn't need to conceal his identity any further. He *knew* he shouldn't be there.
• He registered his guest account using false credentials: "Gary Host" and "Grace Host" - "Ghost"

  • Why wouldn't he just use his real name if he believed what he was doing was legitimate?
• When MIT blocked his IP, he released/renewed and fetched a new one. Fine, no problem on its own, hard to prove intent there. When MIT subsequently blocked his MAC address, he proceeded to change one character and kept on downloading.

  • Computer people will try to reduce this to "MAC addresses aren't legal identifiers blah blah blah." The beliefs of zealous third parties are completely irrelevant: direct measures were taken to prevent his access, he recognized and immediately circumvented them. He *knew* what he was doing. That's what matters.
• Why hide his hardware under boxes? In absence of all of the other facts, sure, one could argue that he didn't want students at this ultra-prestigious Ivy League school to steal his shit, but to a reasonable person weighing the totality of the circumstances: he was again concealing his actions because he knew they were wrong.

I find their post to be a little light on details, but my read is that they're essentially doing what you're complaining they should.

I work on software that Dr and Nurses use. The company I work for trains its own models to provide automated insight on patient history, etc. I've been pretty concerned about these kinds of problems you describe. I sat down with one of the data scientists and talked about biases a while ago. She walked me through the (high level) process they go through to try and detect common biases in the model before publishing.

For example, it is a common belief within the medical community that Black people have higher pain tolerance, and thus don't need as much or as strong of pain killers. People in pain sitting in beds in the ER will be delayed or refused pain killers because of this. This belief has been proven false, but it shows up in papers, notes, etc. and nurses and doctors still will treat their patients as if it's true.

This is just one example of many many things they test for. When training the model the data-science team actually tries to see if they can produce output that exhibit those identified biases/problems and block it from ever been used in production if they do.

I've had people internally tell me how frustrated they are that I or other people aren't letting them get their new-fangled AI-powered feature in front of customers fast enough... Without a lot of discipline and guardrails people would be using ChatGPT or Claude APIs instead.

My point is: I highly doubt that kind of care is being taken in many industries/companies. It's very concerning to me.

- If you mean the actual jurisdictional authority, there are thousands and public records are all over the place.

- Websites aren't generally part of corporate filing records. So the agent would still need a way to connect the website to the corporation even after checking the legitimacy of the corporation.

- Serving the structured info in an HTTP header that is cryptographically verifiable by the browser itself (via its trusted roots) essentially serves as a distributed database for website identity, which eliminates the need for each agent to come up with its own ad-hoc verification system on the fly (and all the additional fetches that come along with it)
